corrected_value.title_o: A mind you can count on: validating breath counting as a behavioral measure of mindfulness

decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding (target 0) identify Levinson et al. (2014), 'A mind you can count on: validating breath counting as a behavioral measure of mindfulness' (doi: 10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01202), as the sole tested original study. Other cited works provide background literature or standard measurement instruments (PVT, MAAS, CFQ, MWQ) and are not replication targets.

decisions.quote:
Our current data support this opinion by replicating some key reliability and validity metrics of the test, as well as demonstrating its applicability in a non-Western setting.
To summarize the findings we replicated the following: BCT performance showed good test-retest reliability, showed a trend correlation with subjectively measured mindfulness (MAAS scores), and a significant correlation with performance on a test of sustained attention.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly conclude that they replicated the key psychometric properties (test-retest reliability, correlation with sustained attention, and association with trait mindfulness on the MAAS) of Levinson et al. (2014). Although the BCT-MAAS correlation was weaker and only significant at the trend level (r = .164, p = .08), a Fisher r-to-z test showed no significant difference from the original estimate (r = .20, z = 0.28, p = .78), and the authors explicitly include it among the replicated findings. The analyses separating miscounts and resets are framed as novel extensions rather than failures of the original study.

decisions.quote: Despite calls for objective measures of mindfulness to be adopted in the field, such practices have not yet become established. Recently, a breath-counting task (BCT) was proposed as a reliable and valid candidate for such an instrument. In this study, we show that the psychometric properties of the BCT are reproducible in a sample of 127 Asian undergraduates.
decisions.reason: The authors collected new empirical data from an independent sample of 127 university students in Singapore to re-test the reliability and validity findings of Levinson et al. (2014), making this a replication.
